title: Anatomy
text: A feed handler turns raw exchange packets into order books your strategies can trust. It sits at the very front of the trading system, so every microsecond it spends, everything downstream inherits.

title: Three jobs
text: An exchange like Nasdaq doesn't send you prices. It sends a stream of events: add this order, execute that one, cancel this one. Each event only makes sense applied in order, to the book you have built so far. Miss one, and the book stays wrong until you notice. So the handler has three jobs. Receive every packet. Put the messages back in sequence. And apply them to the books, fast.

title: Two threads
text: The lab's handler, itch-fh, splits this work across two threads, each pinned to its own core. The rx thread makes every system call. It pulls up to 32 datagrams per call with recvmmsg. It stamps them with the CPU's timestamp counter and copies them into a lock-free ring. The book thread reads that ring. It sequences the messages, decodes ITCH and updates the books, with no system calls, locks or allocation. A third path runs backwards: when a packet is missing, the book thread asks, and the rx thread sends the request.

title: The book loop
text: Here is the book thread's whole loop, from the itch-fh main file. poll takes one packet off the ring and sequences it. deliver applies each in-order message to the books, then records the time since the packet arrived. The loop never sleeps and never blocks: it spins on its own core. Everything it touches was allocated and faulted in before the threads started.

title: One packet
text: Follow one packet. Its header says sequence 1000, with three messages inside. The first is an Add Order: 36 bytes, a buy of 100 shares at 182 dollars 50. 1000 is the sequence the handler expects, so all three are delivered in order. The book thread files the order under its reference number, and adds 100 shares to the 182.50 bid level. In the firm's trader, the same code then pushes a 64 byte top of book update to the trading thread.

title: What breaks
text: What breaks a handler? Slow work on the book thread: one log write or page fault, and packets queue up behind it. A consumer that falls behind: in the lab, a full packet ring drops the packet, and it is recovered like any other loss. And trusting a book after a gap. The lab counts every anomaly, and itch-fh exits with an error unless nothing was lost and every integrity check is zero.

title: Takeaway
text: Receive, sequence, apply. Keep each on its own core, and keep system calls away from the thread that owns the books. The rest of this series takes each piece apart.
